text.title: AI LLM Workload Architecture — Worked Examples
text.summary: One complete spec for a support-ticket summariser, with a note on every value a reader might question, and one spec for the same feature that breaks six subject rules and what the validator and the reviewer say about it.

section.title: Scenario
section.p: A support product summarises inbound tickets with an LLM and lets agents ask follow-up questions over a knowledge-base search tool. A prompt "cleanup" shipped last month and the summaries got vaguer; nobody could say by how much. The team runs steps 1-9 of `content/04-procedure.xml` and lands the spec below with its CI gate.

example.title: Complete spec with judge, budgets, injection cases and fallback
example.note: `scoring.judge.noise_floor` is 0.01 and every tolerance is at least that wide: the judge was run twice at the same commit before thresholds were set, so a 0.02 drop in answer_accuracy is a signal, not judge noise.
`injection_resistance` has tolerance 0.0 and threshold 1.0: a single followed instruction inside a ticket is a failure, so the metric is a hard gate rather than a trend.
`watched_paths` lists four directories, not just the prompts: the last regression came from `config/models.yaml`, which the old path filter did not watch (fm-gate-bypassed-by-config-edit).

Both the production id and the fallback id carry a date suffix; the fallback is a cheaper pinned model rather than a refusal because a stale summary beats no summary for this product, and `deg-429-001` scores its output.
`budgets.per_request` states tokens and cost together: the token ceiling survives a price change, the cost ceiling is what finance signs.
`evidence[]` carries the baseline run, the second run used for the noise floor, and the PR that made the eval job a required check.

section.title: Bad example: the same feature before the spec

example.title: Six subject rules broken
example.note: What the validator prints: `eval_set.path: 'notebooks/eval-playground.ipynb' matches the forbidden not schema` (r-eval-set-version-pinned); `scoring.judge.model_id: 'claude-latest'` fails the pinned-id pattern and `temperature: 0.7 is not the required const 0` (r-scoring-function-deterministic); `regression_gate.blocks_merge: False is not the required const True` and `watched_paths: 1 items is under minItems 2` (r-regression-gate-blocks-merge); `production_model_id: 'gpt-4o-latest'` fails the pattern (r-model-id-pinned); `budgets.measured_in_eval_run: False` (r-latency-and-cost-budgets); `untrusted_input_channels[0].injection_case_ids: 0 items is under minItems 1` (r-injection-cases-in-eval-set); `degradation.retry.max_attempts: 100 is above maximum 10`, `fallback.eval_case_ids: 0 items` and `user_message: length 5 is under minLength 10` (r-degradation-path-defined).

What the reviewer sees beyond the validator: the judge noise floor is 0.06 while the one metric's tolerance is 0.02, so the gate would fire at random even after the judge is pinned; and only the ticket channel is listed although the feature also reads a tool output and a user turn. The spec goes back to step 2 of the procedure.

list.item: Measure the noise floor before setting tolerances; a tolerance tighter than the noise floor turns the gate into a coin flip.
The watched-path list is the gate: every regression that "was not code" lived in a path the filter did not see.
Pinning is one rule applied three times — production model, judge model, fallback model — and the alias sneaks back in whichever one the spec forgot.
